title: Vector & Long-Term Memory
summary: Short-term memory lives in the context window and vanishes when it fills up. Long-term memory stores past facts and turns as embeddings in a vector store, then retrieves only the few most relevant memories on demand — memory as RAG over the conversation. You give the agent explicit write_memory and read_memory tools so it can save durable facts and recall them later, keeping the prompt small while the knowledge grows without bound.

subtopics.title: Short-term memory fills; long-term memory scales
subtopics.explanation: Short-term memory is just the message list you resend each turn, and it is capped by the context window, so old turns eventually get dropped. Long-term memory moves durable facts out of the prompt into a store you can search, so the agent can 'remember' far more than fits in context. This split is the reason serious agents pair a small working context with a large external memory rather than one giant prompt.
subtopics.example:
# short-term: everything the model sees this turn
short_term = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "I'm allergic to peanuts."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Noted."},
]
# this list is capped by the context window and will be trimmed

# long-term: durable facts kept OUTSIDE the prompt, searchable later
long_term_store.save("user is allergic to peanuts")
# next week, with a fresh context, we can still retrieve this fact

subtopics.title: A memory is text plus its embedding
subtopics.explanation: To make memories searchable by meaning, you turn each one into an embedding — a fixed-length vector that places semantically similar text near each other. You store the original text alongside the vector so retrieval can return the human-readable memory, not just numbers. Embedding every memory is the step that turns a pile of notes into something you can query by relevance instead of exact keywords.

subtopics.title: Retrieval is nearest-neighbour by similarity
subtopics.explanation: On each turn you embed the current query and compare it against every stored memory with cosine similarity, keeping the top-k closest. This surfaces memories that are about the same thing even when the words differ, and k stays small so the prompt does not balloon. Ranking by similarity and taking only the top few is exactly RAG, applied to the conversation's own history.

subtopics.title: Expose write_memory and read_memory as tools
subtopics.explanation: Rather than saving everything automatically, you give the agent explicit tools: write_memory(fact) to persist something worth keeping, and read_memory(query) to recall related facts. The model decides when a fact is durable and when it needs to look one up, which keeps the store focused. Making memory a pair of tools puts the save/recall decision inside the same reason-act-observe loop the agent already runs.

subtopics.title: Inject recalled memories back into the prompt
subtopics.explanation: Retrieved memories are only useful if the model actually sees them, so you fold the top-k results into the context as a system or tool message before the model reasons. This grounds the reply in past facts without carrying the entire history. Injecting just the relevant slice is what lets an agent stay personalized and consistent while its working context stays small and cheap.
subtopics.example:
def build_prompt(user_msg: str) -> list[dict]:
    recalled = read_memory(user_msg, k=3)
    return [
        {"role": "system", "content": f"Relevant memories:\n{recalled}"},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
    ]

# the model now answers WITH the recalled facts in view,
# e.g. avoiding peanuts because that memory was retrieved

foundations.overview: An agent's context window is finite, so it cannot simply keep every past turn forever — eventually old information is trimmed and the agent 'forgets'. Long-term memory solves this by moving durable facts out of the prompt into an external vector store: each memory is embedded into a vector, and on each turn the agent embeds the current query, finds the top-k most similar memories with cosine similarity, and injects only those back into context. This is retrieval-augmented generation pointed at the conversation itself. In practice you expose two tools — write_memory to persist a fact and read_memory to recall related ones — so the model decides what is worth keeping and when to look something up, all inside the same reason-act-observe loop. The result is an agent whose working context stays small and cheap while its effective knowledge grows without bound.
foundations.formalDefinition: Long-term agent memory is an external store of (text, embedding) records queried by semantic similarity. On each turn the agent embeds the query, retrieves the top-k records by a similarity metric (e.g. cosine), and injects them into the context; a write path embeds and appends new facts. Exposed as write_memory/read_memory tools, it is RAG whose corpus is the agent's own accumulated facts and turns.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without long-term memory an agent restarts from zero every time context overflows, forgetting user preferences, prior decisions, and facts it just learned. Vector memory lets it stay personalized and consistent across long and repeated interactions while keeping each prompt small, which controls both cost and latency — the difference between a stateless chatbot and an assistant that actually remembers you.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the context window as a tiny desk and the vector store as a huge filing cabinet. The agent can only keep a few papers on the desk at once, so it files durable notes away (write_memory) and, when a new task arrives, pulls just the few folders that match the topic (read_memory) rather than dumping the whole cabinet onto the desk.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Personal assistants recalling your preferences across weeks, support agents remembering a customer's prior tickets, coding agents recalling project conventions, and tutoring agents tracking what a student already learned — all store facts as embeddings and retrieve the relevant few on demand.
foundations.performanceImpact: Retrieval cost is one embedding call for the query plus a similarity scan of the store; a brute-force scan is O(N·d) per turn, so beyond a few thousand memories you switch to an approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HNSW/IVF) for sub-linear lookups. Keeping k small bounds the extra prompt tokens, so recall stays cheap even as the store grows large.
commonUseCases: Personalization: recall user preferences across sessions
Support: retrieve a customer's prior interactions and facts
Coding agents recalling project conventions and decisions
Grounding replies in facts learned earlier in a long task

commonMisconceptions.myth: Long-term memory means stuffing the whole history into the prompt.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The point is the opposite — you keep the prompt small and store history externally, retrieving only the top-k relevant memories per turn so context stays bounded.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should save every message to long-term memory.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Indiscriminate saving fills the store with noise and lowers retrieval precision. The agent (via write_memory) should persist only durable, reusable facts, not every turn.
It returns the most semantically similar records, which can be stale, contradictory, or off-topic. You still filter by relevance/recency and design for wrong hits — retrieval is ranking, not truth.

interactiveExamples.title: Memory as write/read tools inside an agent turn
interactiveExamples.explanation: Wrap the store as write_memory and read_memory tools, then show one turn: the agent recalls relevant facts, injects them into the prompt, and the (faked) model answers grounded in memory. This is RAG over the conversation, driven by the same tool loop the agent already uses.

code.code:
import math

def embed(text: str) -> list[float]:
    keys = ["peanut", "vegetarian", "spicy"]
    t = text.lower()
    return [float(t.count(k)) for k in keys]

STORE = []  # (text, vector) records

def write_memory(fact: str) -> str:
    STORE.append({"text": fact, "vector": embed(fact)})
    return f"saved: {fact}"

def read_memory(query: str, k: int = 2) -> str:
    q = embed(query)
    def cos(v):
        dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(q, v))
        nq = math.sqrt(sum(a * a for a in q)) or 1e-9
        nv = math.sqrt(sum(b * b for b in v)) or 1e-9
        return dot / (nq * nv)
    hits = sorted(STORE, key=lambda r: cos(r["vector"]), reverse=True)[:k]
    return "; ".join(h["text"] for h in hits) or "no relevant memories"

def fake_model(prompt: str) -> str:
    # the 'model' just proves it saw the injected memory
    if "peanut" in prompt.lower():
        return "Recommending a peanut-free dish."
    return "Recommending today's special."

# earlier turns persisted durable facts
write_memory("user is allergic to peanuts")
write_memory("user loves spicy food")

# this turn: recall, inject, then answer
user_msg = "what should I order for dinner?"
recalled = read_memory(user_msg + " allergy peanut", k=1)
prompt = f"Memories: {recalled}\nUser: {user_msg}"
print(fake_model(prompt))
code.caption: read_memory surfaces the allergy fact, it is injected into the prompt, and the model's answer respects it — memory changing the agent's behavior.

theory.question: How does vector-based long-term memory differ from just keeping the whole conversation in the context window?
theory.directAnswer: Keeping the whole conversation in context is short-term memory bounded by the window — it truncates and gets expensive as it grows. Vector long-term memory stores facts as embeddings in an external store and retrieves only the top-k relevant ones per turn, so the prompt stays small while the agent's effective knowledge is unbounded. It is RAG applied to the conversation itself.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An external store of (text, embedding) records queried by semantic similarity, exposed to the agent as write/read tools.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Context windows are finite and costly, so an agent that keeps everything eventually forgets old turns and pays for every token every turn; long-term memory decouples knowledge size from prompt size.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: New facts are embedded and appended; on each turn the query is embedded, the top-k nearest memories are found by cosine similarity, and only those are injected back into the prompt to ground the reply.

theory.whyImportant: It's what lets an agent stay personalized and consistent across long or repeated sessions without the prompt (and its cost) growing without limit.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent stores 'customer runs on the enterprise plan' once; weeks later, on a fresh context, read_memory surfaces that fact so the agent answers correctly without the user repeating it.

followUps.question: Should you save every message to the store?
followUps.answer: No — indiscriminate saving fills the store with noise and hurts retrieval precision. Persist only durable, reusable facts, typically via an explicit write_memory decision.

followUps.question: How do you keep retrieval fast as the store grows?
followUps.answer: A brute-force scan is O(N·d) per turn; beyond a few thousand memories, use an approximate-nearest-neighbour index like HNSW or IVF for sub-linear lookups.

theory.question: Why expose memory as write_memory and read_memory tools rather than saving and injecting everything automatically?
theory.directAnswer: Because the model is best placed to judge what is durable enough to save and when it needs to recall something. Tools put those decisions inside the agent's reason-act-observe loop, keeping the store focused (only reusable facts) and the prompt lean (recall only when relevant), instead of blindly persisting and injecting noise.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two tools — write_memory(fact) that embeds and persists a fact, and read_memory(query) that returns the top-k semantically similar facts — surfaced to the model like any other tool.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Automatic save-everything pollutes the store and lowers precision, while automatic inject-everything defeats the purpose of a bounded context; letting the model choose scopes both.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The model emits a write_memory call when it learns a durable fact and a read_memory call when a task might depend on past knowledge; your code executes the embed/store or embed/rank step and returns the result as an observation.

theory.whyImportant: It aligns memory management with the agent's own reasoning, producing a cleaner store and cheaper prompts than heuristic auto-saving.
theory.realWorldExample: A coding agent calls write_memory('this repo uses 2-space indent') once and later read_memory('formatting conventions') before editing, applying the rule without it ever living permanently in the prompt.

followUps.question: What's a risk of letting the model decide what to save?
followUps.answer: It may over-save or save transient facts; you mitigate with dedup, relevance filters, and periodic hygiene (decay/eviction) on the store.

followUps.question: Can you combine explicit tools with automatic summarization?
followUps.answer: Yes — many systems auto-summarize old turns into the store as a background write while still exposing explicit read_memory for on-demand recall.

scenario.question: An assistant with vector memory keeps giving stale or contradictory answers as its store grows to tens of thousands of memories. How do you diagnose and fix retrieval quality?
scenario.directAnswer: Treat it as a retrieval-precision problem: measure what read_memory returns for failing queries, then attack causes — dedup near-identical memories, add recency/relevance filtering so newer facts win over stale ones, tighten k, add metadata filters (user id, topic), and switch to an ANN index for scale. Keep a hygiene job to decay or evict outdated memories.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A quality-and-scale problem where similarity search surfaces the wrong or outdated memories into the prompt.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Unbounded, duplicated, and contradictory memories lower precision; pure cosine similarity ignores recency, so a stale fact can outrank the current one, and a huge flat store also slows lookups.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Log the top-k for failing turns, cluster duplicates and dedup on write, add a recency or confidence score to the ranking, filter by user/topic metadata before ranking, and reconcile contradictions (keep the newest or highest-confidence fact) via a periodic hygiene pass.

scenario.whyImportant: It connects vector memory directly to answer correctness and cost, showing a metrics-driven approach rather than blindly adding more memories.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs showed an old 'user is vegetarian' memory outranking a newer 'user now eats fish'; adding recency weighting and a dedup/eviction pass made the current fact win and stopped the contradictions.

followUps.question: How would recency weighting change the ranking?
followUps.answer: Blend similarity with a time-decay term so a slightly-less-similar but newer memory can outrank an older one, preventing stale facts from dominating.

followUps.question: Why add metadata filters before similarity search?
followUps.answer: Filtering by user id or topic first shrinks the candidate set to relevant memories, improving both precision and speed versus ranking the entire store.

coding.question: Implement a VectorMemory class with write(text, vector) and search(query_vec, k) that returns the top-k texts by cosine similarity, safely handling zero-magnitude vectors.
coding.thoughtProcess: I store each memory as a (text, vector) record on write. For search I compute cosine similarity of the query against every record, guarding the denominator so an all-zero vector yields 0.0 rather than crashing, then sort descending and slice the top-k. A list slice is naturally safe when k exceeds the store size, so no extra bounds check is needed.
lineByLine: write appends a (text, vector) record so the human-readable memory travels with its embedding.
_cosine computes dot product over paired components and the two magnitudes.
The na == 0 or nb == 0 guard returns 0.0 for zero-magnitude vectors, avoiding a divide-by-zero.
search sorts all records by similarity to the query, highest first.
The [:k] slice returns the top-k texts and is safe even when k exceeds the number of records.
The __main__ block writes two facts and shows the peanut memory ranking first for a near-aligned query.
coding.timeComplexity: O(N·d) per search — a similarity scan over N memories of dimension d (use an ANN index for large N).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(N·d) to hold all memory vectors, plus O(N) for the ranking.

followUps.question: How would you scale search beyond a brute-force scan?
followUps.answer: Replace the linear scan with an approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HNSW/IVF) or a vector database, trading exactness for sub-linear query time.

followUps.question: How would you add recency to the ranking?
followUps.answer: Store a timestamp per record and combine similarity with a time-decay factor in the sort key so newer memories are favored on ties or near-ties.

keyTakeaways: Short-term memory is the context window (bounded); long-term memory is an external vector store (unbounded) queried by similarity.
Each memory is stored as text plus its embedding; retrieval embeds the query and returns the top-k nearest by cosine similarity — RAG over the conversation.
Expose memory as write_memory/read_memory tools so the model decides what to persist and when to recall, keeping the store focused and the prompt lean.
Inject only the top-k recalled memories back into context so the agent stays personalized while the working prompt stays small and cheap.
At scale, use an ANN index and memory hygiene (dedup, recency, eviction) to keep retrieval fast, precise, and free of stale or contradictory facts.
